claim_text: ADHD-related executive difficulties can begin in childhood.
ADHD-related executive difficulties can persist through adolescence.
ADHD-related executive difficulties can persist into adulthood.
Persistent ADHD traits can impair more than one life setting.
Adult difficulties may instead begin after mood, sleep, trauma, substance, medication, or occupational changes.
High academic or intellectual achievement is compatible with clinically meaningful impairment.
Higher intelligence can delay recognition of ADHD or autistic impairment.
Compensation can preserve achievement while increasing effort or instability.
Achievement alone does not establish compensation or masking.
Observed achievement may reflect efficient independent functioning rather than hidden impairment.
Interest can moderate attention or task performance in ADHD.
Novelty can moderate attention or task performance in ADHD.
Reward and immediate feedback can moderate ADHD task performance.
Urgency or deadlines can alter task initiation or performance.
Motivational effects may be nonspecific rather than unique to ADHD.
Checklists and reminders can improve real-world task performance.
ADHD coaching or executive-function-focused CBT can improve functioning.
Digital aids or assistive technology can support executive functioning.
Occupational or educational redesign can reduce functional impairment.
AI-assisted organization has evidence for durable clinical benefit.
External scaffolds can have limited durability, dependence, burden, or harms.
ADHD is associated with social and peer difficulties.
Autistic features can explain additional social-communication variance beyond ADHD.
Anxiety, trauma, mood state, substances, or conflict can explain social difficulties.
Multiple interacting conditions may explain social difficulties better than one diagnosis.
Person-environment fit can moderate neurodevelopmental impairment.
Autonomy, meaning, or task fit can improve functioning.
Standardized or repetitive demands can amplify impairment.
Severity, burnout, workload, or interpersonal conflict may explain apparent mismatch effects.
Short or inadequate sleep can worsen attention and executive functioning.
Sleep quality and circadian irregularity can worsen ADHD-related functioning.
Shift work can impair sleep, cognition, or mood.
Within-person symptom variation can track sleep changes.
Sleep loss can precipitate or amplify bipolar-spectrum mood symptoms.
Some apparent sleep effects may reflect reverse causation from mood or baseline severity.
Mood episodes can produce episodic executive, speech, salience, and impulse-control changes.
Cannabis or THC can worsen cognition, anxiety, psychosis risk, or mood stability.
Prescription stimulants can produce state-dependent activation or mood effects.
Nicotine can produce acute activation and dependence-related state changes.
Medication effects can mimic or amplify baseline neurodevelopmental traits.
Sleep, mood, cannabis, stimulants, and nicotine can interact.
Stable persistence during euthymia, abstinence, and adequate sleep supports a trait-level component.
Maladaptive or immersive daydreaming is associated with loneliness, rejection, shame, or boredom.
Daydreaming can function as emotional compensation or escape.
Temporal direction between adversity and daydreaming is established.
Normative fantasy, dissociation, compulsivity, trauma, or mood can better explain daydreaming.
ADHD or autistic traits are associated with divergent thinking.
ADHD or autistic traits are associated with real-world creativity.
Hyperfocus is a reliable and clinically meaningful construct.
ADHD or autistic traits are associated with superior pattern recognition.
Proposed strengths and impairments can represent context-dependent trade-offs.
Education, intelligence, personality, mood, or selection bias can explain proposed strengths.
ADHD and developmental coordination disorder commonly overlap.
Developmental coordination difficulties can persist into adulthood.
Motor impairment can exceed what inattention alone explains.
Neurologic disease, injury, anxiety, medication, obesity, or limited practice can explain motor problems.
Anxiety, shame, rejection, or bullying are associated with functional burden.
Anxiety or rejection-related distress mediates avoidance or social dysfunction.
Prospective evidence establishes the direction of this mediation.
Functional difficulty can remain independently associated with neurodevelopmental traits.
Baseline traits and state or environmental modifiers interact.
Context-dependent compensation can alter observable impairment.
One coherent adaptive-constraint model explains the observations better than alternatives.
Retrospective reconstruction and confirmation bias can create apparent coherence.
Multiple independent or interacting causes can outperform one unifying model.
Group-level literature cannot establish individual diagnosis or causation.
